submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the subword piece that opens a word or a character and is left incomplete by it: in Latin/Cyrillic text the short fragment the byte-pair tokenizer splits off the front of a long, mostly Greco-Latin technical word (' non', ' co', ' re', ' pre', ' poly', ' dys', ' dyst', ' hyper', ' micro', ' multi', ' syn', ' tele', ' anti', ' meta', ' proto', ' pale', ' gastro', ' electro', ' psycho', ' pseudo', ' retro', ' пер', ' gre', ' Edu'), and in CJK/Indic/Greek text the invalid-UTF-8 lead-byte pair of a character (the '�' tokens, e.g. bytes e5 8b or e0 ae); it reaches 0.3-1.0 of max there, and the same word fires or goes silent purely on where the tokenizer splits it (spectro-photometric 0.61 of max vs spectrophotometric 0.07; 務 as a byte pair 0.91 vs 务 as one token 0.16). It stays near zero (mean <0.1 of max, only 2-3% of tokens firing) on complete one-token words whether common or technical ('the', 'of', 'to', 'in', 'is', 'national', 'medical', 'immunohistochemical'), on word-internal continuation pieces ('xs' in coxsackievirus, 'okers', ' night', ' wind', ' dent'), and on native-English prefixes ('over-', 'out-', 'under-'); it rises only part-way (0.3-0.9) on the hyphen of a compound or on ' and'/'or' inside a technical noun phrase ('vertebrate and insect', 'the heart and the lungs'), and not at all on ' and' joining verbs ('she smiled and waved' ~0).

rival_explanations: Any subword fragment triggers it, so the opening pieces of ordinary native compounds and long native words (' night' in nightingale, ' wind' in windmill, ' dent' in dentistry, ' thunder' in thunderstorm) should fire as strongly as ' non' and ' poly'.

The trigger class is exactly a closed list of Greco-Latin prefixes plus the non-ASCII byte fragments, so unseen combining forms (' hex', ' oct', ' prot', ' pale', 'ozo') and the hyphen/' and'/' the' cases should not fire at all.

It is a technical-register detector that fires wherever scientific prose is dense, so ordinary complete technical words ('national', 'medical', 'spectrophotometric') and function words inside a science paragraph should also fire strongly.

Flying on Hydrogen
An unmanned aerial vehicle powered by fuel cells running on compressed hydrogen is one of the most innovative developments to fly out of GTRI and Georgia Tech's Aerospace Systems Design Laboratory. The project was spearheaded by David Parekh, GTRI’s former deputy director and founder of Georgia Tech’s Center for Innovative Fuel Cell and Battery Technologies.
Parekh wanted to develop a vehicle that would both advance fuel cell technology and galvanize industry interest. "A fuel cell aircraft is more compelling than just a lab demonstration, or even a fuel cell system powering a house," Parekh explained. The automotive industry has made strides with fuel cells. But apart from spacecraft, little has been done to leverage fuel cell technology for aerospace applications.
Fuel cells, which create an electrical current when they convert hydrogen and oxygen into water, are attractive as energy sources because of their high energy density. Higher energy density translates into longer endurance.
The proton-exchange membrane system that flies the 22-foot wingspan aircraft generates only 500 watts. “Five hundred watts is plenty of power for a light bulb, but not for the propulsion system of an aircraft this size,” said research engineer Adam Broughton.
Although fuel cells don’t produce enough power for the propulsion systems of commercial passenger aircraft, they could power smaller, slower vehicles like unmanned aerial vehicles and provide a low-cost alternative to satellites. Such aircraft could also track hurricanes, patrol borders and conduct general reconnaissance.
Other research groups have also demonstrated hydrogen-powered unmanned aerial vehicles, but these aircraft were either very small or used liquid hydrogen. Compressed hydrogen, which is what the automotive industry is using, is cheaper and easier to work with.
Georgia Tech’s demonstrator vehicle operates like a full-sized aircraft, requiring no auxiliary batteries or boosters for take-off. The smaller planes had no landing gear and had to be hand launched.

De tribute to the legendendary music of Status Quo
Status Quo tributeband Back to Back is direct na hun oprichting eind 2016, een graag geziene band op festivals, in zalen en poppodia. De door de wol geverfde bandleden hebben dan ook allemaal hun sporen allang verdiend in de muziek scene.
Ze presenteren een heerlijk repertoire aan Quo nummers uit de tijd voor “In the army now”. De Herkenbare intro’s, stevige gitaarriffs, scheurende solo’s, stampende drumbeat en natuurlijk de onmiskenbare meerstemmige zangpartijen. Status Quo maar dan ook echt op en top Status Quo! De bekenden hits komen voorbij naar ook vele albumtracks waar Status Quo fans een groot plezier mee gedaan wordt.
Sound-and-look-alike!
Frontman Daniel Roumen lijkt en klinkt qua stem, gitaarspel en uiterlijk op Francis Rossi in zijn jongere jaren. Mede muzikanten Edwin Kappe (gitaar), Frenk Aendenroomer (bas en zang) en Hans Lemmen (Drum en zang) zijn Quo fans van het eerste uur. En stuk voor stuk ervaren muzikanten die weten hoe ze hun Status Quo feestje op elk popdium moeten bouwen. De band heeft in no-time een stevige naam opgebouwd nationaal en internationaal. De band speelde zo onder andere al op de Duitse Status Quo fanclub meeting. Back to Back laat je Status Quo beleven alsof je aanwezig bent bij de oorspronkelijke helden van weleer.
Stil blijven staan is onmogelijk bij deze band die iedereen mee terugneemt naar de tijd dat Status Quo nog een Top 40 kanon was.

[Influence of air pollution on pregnant women's health and pregnancy outcomes].

UNLABELLED
Outdoor and indoor air pollution pollutants can be a potential cause to a lot of negative effects on the health of pregnant women and outcome of pregnancy. The objective of this paper was to estimate the influence of outdoor and indoor air pollution on the health of pregnant women and outcome of pregnancy.


MATERIAL AND METHODS
The study subjects were the pregnant women, non-smokers, who were not professionally exposed to air pollution. They were divided into the exposed group (n = 189) and control group (n = 178) during the exposure to outdoor air pollution. The data on exposure to sources of indoor air pollution (smoke produced by burning fossil fuels and passive smoking) during pregnancy were obtained from the questionnaire. Data on health condition and outcome of pregnancy were obtained from medical records of tested pregnant women.


RESULTS
The research results have shown that the frequency of anemia (OR = 6.76; 95% CI = 1.28-7.72), upper respiratory symptoms (OR = 9.53; 95% CI = 1.32-3.8) and bleeding (OR = 20.5; 95% CI = 2.03-6.97) was significantly higher in pregnant women exposed to outdoor air pollution as compared with the control group. The occurrence of upper respiratory symptoms (OR = 40.42; 95% CI = 2.96-8.91) and bleeding (OR = 53.21; 95% CI = 4.3-15.73) was significantly higher in pregnant women who had been exposed to fossil fuel smoke. Exposure to passive smoking had significant influence on the development of upper respiratory symptoms (OR = 34.58; 95% CI = 3.05-11.66).

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s administration is close to a decision on how to regulate the burgeoning natural gas industry seeking drilling rights across the upstate region of New York.
Hydraulic fracturing, known more commonly as fracking, is used to extract natural gas from shale rock located miles below the earth’s surface. When a drilling company “fracks” a well, it injects large quantities of sand, water and chemicals into the ground, creating fissures in the sediment that release the gas trapped deep inside. The Marcellus Shale, one of the largest shale formations, lies primarily underneath parts of New York and Pennsylvania, a state where companies — spurred on by the support of Republican Governor Tom Corbett — have drilled rigs on rural land by the hundreds.
Despite industry promises that the hydraulic fracturing process is safe, critics contend that the potential environmental impacts posed by natural gas drilling are not worth what they say may be short-lived economic gains.

One team measured the ratio of magnesium to calcium in each shell fragment, a proxy for temperature at the time of deposition. readings.explanation: The pole fires on the subword piece that opens a word or a character and is left incomplete by it: in Latin/Cyrillic text the short fragment the byte-pair tokenizer splits off the front of a long, mostly Greco-Latin technical word (' non', ' co', ' re', ' pre', ' poly', ' dys', ' dyst', ' hyper', ' micro', ' multi', ' syn', ' tele', ' anti', ' meta', ' proto', ' pale', ' gastro', ' electro', ' psycho', ' pseudo', ' retro', ' пер', ' gre', ' Edu'), and in CJK/Indic/Greek text the invalid-UTF-8 lead-byte pair of a character (the '�' tokens, e.g. bytes e5 8b or e0 ae); it reaches 0.3-1.0 of max there, and the same word fires or goes silent purely on where the tokenizer splits it (spectro-photometric 0.61 of max vs spectrophotometric 0.07; 務 as a byte pair 0.91 vs 务 as one token 0.16). It stays near zero (mean <0.1 of max, only 2-3% of tokens firing) on complete one-token words whether common or technical ('the', 'of', 'to', 'in', 'is', 'national', 'medical', 'immunohistochemical'), on word-internal continuation pieces ('xs' in coxsackievirus, 'okers', ' night', ' wind', ' dent'), and on native-English prefixes ('over-', 'out-', 'under-'); it rises only part-way (0.3-0.9) on the hyphen of a compound or on ' and'/'or' inside a technical noun phrase ('vertebrate and insect', 'the heart and the lungs'), and not at all on ' and' joining verbs ('she smiled and waved' ~0).

Any subword fragment triggers it, so the opening pieces of ordinary native compounds and long native words (' night' in nightingale, ' wind' in windmill, ' dent' in dentistry, ' thunder' in thunderstorm) should fire as strongly as ' non' and ' poly'.

The trigger class is exactly a closed list of Greco-Latin prefixes plus the non-ASCII byte fragments, so unseen combining forms (' hex', ' oct', ' prot', ' pale', 'ozo') and the hyphen/' and'/' the' cases should not fire at all.

It is a technical-register detector that fires wherever scientific prose is dense, so ordinary complete technical words ('national', 'medical', 'spectrophotometric') and function words inside a science paragraph should also fire strongly.
